chapter.title: Setting Up a React Project
chapter.description: The realistic ways to start a React project today, and what each one gives you.

blocks.text: You do not have to configure a build system by hand. There are a few standard starting points, and which one you pick depends on what you are building.
Vite: the fast default for a single page app

blocks.code:
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
blocks.caption: A React app running locally in well under a minute.

blocks.text: Vite gives you a dev server with instant reloads and a production build command. It is the usual choice when you want a plain client-side React app with no server rendering.
Next.js: React with routing and server rendering

blocks.code:
npx create-next-app@latest my-app
cd my-app
npm run dev
blocks.caption: Next.js adds file-based routing, server rendering and data fetching.

blocks.text: If your project needs good SEO, server rendering, or an API layer alongside the UI, a framework such as Next.js saves you from assembling those pieces yourself.
What the generated project contains

items: `index.html` - a single page with an empty `<div id="root">` for React to fill.
`src/main.jsx` - the entry point, where React attaches itself to that div.

blocks.caption: src/main.jsx - the whole bridge between React and the page.

blocks.text: `react` holds the component model. `react-dom` is the renderer that targets a browser. That split is why React Native can reuse the same component model with a different renderer.
No build step at all
For experimenting you can load React straight from a CDN in a plain HTML file. That is exactly what the code exercises on this site do: your code runs in a sandboxed frame with React already loaded.

blocks.text: To use React well it helps to know roughly what happens between your code and the pixels on screen. You do not need the internals, just the shape of the process.
Elements are plain objects
When you write JSX, you are not creating DOM nodes. You are creating small plain JavaScript objects that describe what you want. These are called React **elements**.

blocks.caption: A React element is a cheap description, not a DOM node.

blocks.text: Because elements are just objects, creating them is fast and throwing them away costs almost nothing. That is what makes the next step affordable.
Rendering and reconciliation

A **render** is React calling your components to get a fresh tree of elements. React then compares that new tree with the previous one and works out the smallest set of real DOM changes needed. That comparison step is called **reconciliation**, and the in-memory tree is often called the **virtual DOM**.

items: Something changes: a user event, a state update, or new props from a parent.
React calls the affected components again, producing a new element tree.
React diffs the new tree against the previous one.
React applies only the differences to the real DOM. This is the **commit**.

blocks.text: The virtual DOM is not magically fast. Touching the real DOM is what is slow, so React does as little of it as possible and does it in one batch.
Why the whole component re-runs

A common surprise for newcomers is that when state changes, React calls your entire component function again from the top. Every line runs, every variable is recreated. Only the DOM updates are minimal, not the function calls.
This is why React components should be predictable: given the same props and state, they should produce the same output, and they should not change things outside themselves while rendering.
Do not mutate variables, write to the DOM, or start network requests directly in the body of a component. Those belong in event handlers or effects, which you will meet later.

next.title: Your First Component
next.description: Write, render and edit a real React component in the browser.

blocks.text: A component is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns something React can render. That is the entire rule.
Why the capital letter matters

JSX uses the case of the tag name to decide what you meant. A lowercase tag such as `<div>` is treated as a built-in HTML element. A capitalised tag such as `<Welcome>` is treated as a reference to a component variable in scope.
If your component renders nothing and the browser console complains about an unrecognised tag, check the capital letter first. It is the most common beginner mistake.
Rendering a component
Components only appear on screen once something renders them. At the top of the tree, `createRoot` connects React to a DOM node; below that, components render each other.

blocks.title: Write your first component
blocks.instructions: Make the Greeting component return an h1 that says exactly: Hello, React!

tests.name: The text is inside an h1 element

blocks.text: Change the text and run it again. Notice that you never told React to update the heading - you changed the description and React did the rest.
What you have learned

items: React is a library for describing user interfaces rather than instructing the DOM.
JSX produces plain objects called elements; React diffs them and updates the DOM minimally.
Vite or Next.js will set up a working project for you in one command.
A component is a capitalised function that returns renderable output.
